source.title: Learning Towards Emergence: Paving the Way to Induce Emergence by Inhibiting Monosemantic Neurons on Pre-trained Models
source.authors: Jia-Chuan Wang; Shimin Di; Tianhao Tang; Hao-Yang Li; Charles Wang Wai Ng; Xiao-Fang Zhou; Lei Chen

page_placements.theme: Scale and fine-tuning trends in neuron monosemanticity proxies

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is present, though some figure data are only available as plots.
record.tranche_reason: Measures monosemanticity across Pythia model scales using MS-based statistics, rather than estimating the claim’s shares of neuron poles with one or more jobs.
record.gate_note: The scale analysis reports K-S statistics for three feature datasets in Figure 4; the plotted point values are not stated numerically. The text says the statistics decrease as model scale increases. FKR results and performance after deliberately inhibiting neurons do not measure the claimed shares of interpretable neuron poles, so they are not recorded as rows for these versions.
record.test_reason: The study measures how distinct a neuron's activation-variance (MS) score is for its best label among 9 fixed dataset labels, across Pythia 70M–6.9B. That is a related but different construct from V2's share of neuron poles with one main job, so its results do not test any version. A falling K-S statistic cannot show whether ~90% of neurons have one main job: neurons may track features outside the 9 labels. The authors also say the results depend heavily on the feature dataset. The rest of the paper deliberately inhibits neurons during training (L2E) and reports task accuracy, which is not a rate of the behaviour.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors say sparse probing validates MS and that MS-based analyses show monosemanticity falling with scale; FKR rising with scale is presented as further support. They report that L2E, regularization-style inhibition of the top 2% MS neurons in middle layers during shortened pretraining, gains about 1–5% on ARC-C, PIQA and SciQ. They caution that results on MMLU, BBL and ARC-Easy are mixed or negative.
record.recipe_differences: Uses sparse probing and an MS-based scale analysis, not an audit of pole-level job counts or explanations tested on held-out activations.
record.method_sensitivity: The scale analysis uses three feature datasets; the authors report anomalous Code Language results for the 70M model and emphasize that results depend on feature-dataset quality.

fits_no_version.finding: In Pythia 70M–6.9B, the K-S statistic between MS scores on a neuron's best-label inputs and on all inputs decreases with scale, for 3 feature datasets (Fig. 4, values plotted only). Mean best-label MS is also lower in larger models across layers (Figs. 5, 9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation-variance concentration on one of a fixed set of labelled features declines as dense LM scale grows (Pythia 70M–6.9B).

fits_no_version.finding: False Killing Rate at a fixed inhibition percentage rises with model scale and peaks in middle layers (Figs. 6, 11). It reaches 67% for 70M on Code Language at 1% inhibition, which the authors take as a weak-dataset artifact.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Label-based monosemanticity proxies depend strongly on feature-dataset quality, and their scale trend is confounded by it.

record.problems: The study uses Pythia models and feature datasets rather than pole-level job counts; the scale evidence is presented in plots without numeric values in the text. The authors note that monosemanticity analysis depends heavily on feature-dataset quality, that probing is less effective for some Code Language results, and that training experiments use only 10% of the original Pythia training steps.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted due to the 60-row cap. Performance results after deliberately inhibiting selected neurons, FKR, and MS-validation comparisons are not rows for the tested share-of-interpretable-neurons version because they do not measure the claimed shares.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B pole audit or job-count shares.
No shares of neurons with one or two jobs in any model; no MoE models; nothing above 6.9B.
No vision models or recursive-generalization analysis.
No comparison of architectures or tools.
No test of explanations' predictive accuracy.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The reader's V2 limits_scope label is removed. The measure is a relative MS distinctiveness against 9 Gurnee et al. labels, not a share of interpretable neurons, and the authors stress dependence on dataset quality. Only the Natural Language dataset probes reliably.

versions.untested_parts: Does not estimate the proportions of Qwen3-32B neuron poles with one job, two related jobs, or jobs not yet understood.
Tests Pythia scales from 70M to 6.9B with MS-based proxies, not shares of poles. Does not test MoE models or models up to trillions of parameters.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron or recursive-generalization analysis.
Does not compare architecture or tool changes, or estimate interpretability shares in InceptionV1-sized vision models.
Does not test attribution graphs or whether neurons alone suffice as circuit units.
Does not test explanations against held-out activating examples or measure prediction failures.
Does not score neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

rows.locator_found: Figure 4, Section 3.2; Appendix B.1 (Figure 10 discussion) calls 70M Code Language results abnormal, including Figure 4

relation.reason: It analyses monosemanticity across scale to motivate its own inhibition method (L2E). It does not test any version of the claim.

tranche.reason: The study measures a variance-based MS score for each neuron's best feature among 9 fixed dataset labels. That is a different construct from V2's share of neuron poles with one main job, so it tests no version (fits_no_version).

source_check.notes: All 18 rows are K-S points that appear only in Fig. 4, with no values in the text, so cannot_determine and versions none fit. The authors flag 70M Code Language as abnormal because probing F1 was weak, and they note weak feature datasets (FKR 21.8% for Data Subset, 67% for Code Language at 1% inhibition on 70M).

statements.correction: Pythia 70M, 160M, 410M, 1B, 2.8B and 6.9B, with 1,000 random neurons per scale. The K-S statistic between MS scores on the best feature (ℓ*) and on all inputs falls with scale on Natural Language, Data Subset and Code Language (Fig. 4, plotted only; each dataset has 9 features). Mean ℓ* MS drops with scale (Fig. 5 for Natural Language, Fig. 9 for the other two). The authors call the 70M Code Language results abnormal, including in Fig. 4.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Pythia scale sweep from 70M to 6.9B across Natural Language, Data Subset, and Code Language datasets
reader_labels.reason: The authors report declining K-S statistics as scale increases, suggesting weaker prominence of relatively monosemantic features in this tested range; the measure is not a share of neuron poles and the plotted values are not numerically stated (r1–r18).
